# SMOTE {#sec-imbalenced-smote}

::: {style="visibility: hidden; height: 0px;"}
## SMOTE
:::

The goal of the Synthetic minority oversampling technique (SMOTE) is to deal with imbalanced data using synthetically generated samples [@chawla2002smote].

this method is in a way similar to [up-sampling](imbalenced-upsample.qmd),
But there is a twist.
Instead of sampling observations from the minority classes,
We instead generate new observations based on the characteristics of the data set.

Generally works for categorical outcomes (hence imbalance),
and the base case only works with numeric data with no missingness.

We start by identifying the minority classes and the majority class.
counting how many observations are in each, as this will be used as a target for how many observations to generate.

Between each minority class, you calculate all the nearest neighbors.
Then, for each observation, you are randomly picking one of its close neighbors (typically `k= 5`) as its designated neighbor for the task.
Then a synthetic observation is generated at random on the line between these two points. 
This is typically done for every observation.
With multiple runs, depending on how many observations will need to be created.
A different random neighbor is picked each time, as well as a random point on the spanning line.

You generally have a ratio threshold,
determining how many observations you need.
If you want a precise match for the counts of observations, you can randomly select observations to generate during the last run for a precise number of generated observations.

@fig-imbalenced-smote walks through the whole procedure on a small two-dimensional data set.

```{r}
#| label: fig-imbalenced-smote
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5.6
#| fig-cap: |
#|   SMOTE generates each new observation by interpolating between a minority
#|   observation and one of its nearest minority neighbors.
#| fig-alt: |
#|   Four scatter plots in a 2x2 grid, each showing the same two-dimensional
#|   data set with a large gray majority class in the lower left and a smaller
#|   pink minority class in the upper right. Panel 1: one minority point is
#|   enlarged to mark it as the point being processed. Panel 2: a dashed circle
#|   around that point encloses its five nearest minority neighbors, which are
#|   drawn as hollow triangles. Panel 3: one neighbor is picked and a new
#|   hollow point appears partway along the straight line between the pair.
#|   Panel 4: the process has been repeated, and the minority region is now
#|   filled with synthetic points so that both classes have the same size.
source("imbalenced-diagrams.R")

imb_data <- imb_toy()
minority <- which(imb_data$class == "minority")

focus <- minority[which.min((imb_data$x[minority] - 2.6)^2 + (imb_data$y[minority] - 1.9)^2)]
neighbors <- imb_neighbors(imb_data, focus, minority, k = 5)

focus_point <- imb_data[focus, ]
neighbor_points <- imb_data[neighbors, ]

# The most distant of the five, so the interpolation is visible at print size.
picked <- neighbors[which.max(
  (neighbor_points$x - focus_point$x)^2 + (neighbor_points$y - focus_point$y)^2
)]
picked_point <- imb_data[picked, ]

synth_point <- imb_interpolate(imb_data, focus, picked, gap = 0.45)
radius <- imb_radius(imb_data, focus, neighbors)

p1 <- imb_base(imb_data, "1. Pick a point from the minority class") +
  geom_point(data = focus_point, size = 4.5, shape = 17, show.legend = FALSE)

p2 <- imb_base(imb_data, "2. Find its k nearest minority neighbors") +
  geom_path(
    data = imb_ring(focus_point, radius), aes(x, y),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, color = imb_colors[["minority"]],
    linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  geom_point(data = neighbor_points, size = 3.5, shape = 2, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_point(data = focus_point, size = 4.5, shape = 17, show.legend = FALSE)

p3 <- imb_base(imb_data, "3. Interpolate towards one of them") +
  geom_segment(
    data = data.frame(
      x = focus_point$x, y = focus_point$y,
      xend = picked_point$x, yend = picked_point$y
    ),
    aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, color = imb_colors[["minority"]], linewidth = 0.4
  ) +
  geom_point(data = picked_point, size = 4.5, shape = 17, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_point(data = focus_point, size = 4.5, shape = 17, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_point(data = synth_point, size = 4.5, shape = 2, stroke = 0.9,
             show.legend = FALSE)

p4 <- imb_base(imb_smote(imb_data), "4. Repeat until the classes are balanced")

# Only the last panel contributes the legend; the earlier panels have no
# synthetic points, so their keys would come out blank.
no_legend <- guides(color = "none", shape = "none")

((p1 + no_legend) + (p2 + no_legend)) / ((p3 + no_legend) + p4) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

One of the major shortcomings is that the base algorithm is limited to numeric predictors with no missing values,
making it hard to use in many cases.

This algorithm has no notion of data quality,
meaning that bad data quality can make for some really unfortunate samples,
especially for lone outliers.
@fig-imbalenced-smote-outlier follows a single stray minority observation through the same procedure.
Its nearest minority neighbors are all the way across the majority class,
so the interpolation runs straight through territory where no minority observation was ever seen,
and the synthetic points land in the middle of the majority class.

It also treats the observations of each class by itself.
While this is computationally and conceptually faster,
it is a much simpler data representation,
one that doesn't use any information about their interactions.
Furthermore, it includes no information about the majority class,
which may otherwise be helpful to guide the method.
This is the second thing @fig-imbalenced-smote-outlier shows:
the majority observations in the way of the interpolation are visible to us, but not to the algorithm.
Nothing in SMOTE consults them, so nothing stops the bridge from being built.

```{r}
#| label: fig-imbalenced-smote-outlier
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5.6
#| fig-cap: |
#|   A single outlying minority observation is enough to make SMOTE generate
#|   synthetic observations inside the majority class.
#| fig-alt: |
#|   Four scatter plots in a 2x2 grid showing the same data set as the previous
#|   figure, where one minority point sits alone in the lower left, far below
#|   the gray majority cloud and far from the rest of the pink minority class
#|   in the upper right. Panel 1: that lone point is enlarged. Panel 2: five
#|   long lines connect it to its nearest minority neighbors, all of which are
#|   on the other side of the majority class. Panel 3: hollow synthetic points
#|   are placed along those lines, landing on top of the majority cloud.
#|   Panel 4: the majority points that the new synthetic points now sit among
#|   are ringed, showing that the algorithm never looked at them.
outlier <- which.min(imb_data$y)
outlier_point <- imb_data[outlier, ]
outlier_neighbors <- imb_neighbors(imb_data, outlier, minority, k = 5)

spokes <- data.frame(
  x = outlier_point$x,
  y = outlier_point$y,
  xend = imb_data$x[outlier_neighbors],
  yend = imb_data$y[outlier_neighbors]
)

set.seed(2)
bridge <- do.call(rbind, lapply(
  outlier_neighbors,
  function(j) imb_interpolate(imb_data, outlier, j, gap = runif(3, 0.2, 0.7))
))

# The majority points the new observations have been dropped on top of.
to_bridge <- vapply(seq_len(nrow(imb_data)), function(i) {
  min(sqrt((bridge$x - imb_data$x[i])^2 + (bridge$y - imb_data$y[i])^2))
}, numeric(1))

swallowed <- which(imb_data$class == "majority" & to_bridge < 0.4)

o1 <- imb_base(imb_data, "1. A minority point far from its own class") +
  geom_point(data = outlier_point, size = 4.5, shape = 17, show.legend = FALSE)

o2 <- imb_base(imb_data, "2. Its nearest minority neighbors are far away") +
  geom_segment(
    data = spokes, aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, color = imb_colors[["minority"]], linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  geom_point(data = imb_data[outlier_neighbors, ], size = 3.5, shape = 2,
             show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_point(data = outlier_point, size = 4.5, shape = 17, show.legend = FALSE)

o3 <- imb_base(imb_data, "3. The synthetic points land in between") +
  geom_segment(
    data = spokes, aes(x = x, y = y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
    inherit.aes = FALSE, color = imb_colors[["minority"]], linewidth = 0.3
  ) +
  geom_point(data = bridge, size = 3, shape = 2, stroke = 0.9,
             show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_point(data = outlier_point, size = 4.5, shape = 17, show.legend = FALSE)

bridge$id <- NA_integer_

o4 <- imb_base(rbind(imb_data, bridge),
               "4. The majority points were never consulted") +
  geom_point(data = imb_data[swallowed, ], aes(x, y), inherit.aes = FALSE,
             shape = 1, size = 4, stroke = 0.7, color = imb_removed)

((o1 + no_legend) + (o2 + no_legend)) / ((o3 + no_legend) + o4) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect") &
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Since we are using a nearest neighbor search,
We have a hyperparameter `k` that is used to denote how many observations should be considered for pairs.

The nearest neighbor search is central to the SMOTE method and thus responsible for many of the downsides associated with the method.
One of the problems is that the idea of nearest neighbors becomes more fuzzy as we enter higher dimensions.
This will naturally extend to how SMOTE becomes applicable. 
Similarly, the nearest neighbor search is also responsible for the high computational cost that can occur when the data becomes larger.
computational cost

Many of the different issues are addressed by some of the [SMOTE variants](imbalenced-smote-variants.qmd).

Base SMOTE needs no expanding to handle more than two classes, as described in @sec-imbalenced-multiclass.

Like all the methods in this section, this changes the distribution of the training data set, which is covered in @sec-imbalenced-distribution.

## R Examples

```{r}
#| label: ames
#| echo: false
#| message: false
set.seed(1234)
```

We will be using the same subset of the `ames` data set as in the [up-sampling](imbalenced-upsample.qmd) chapter.
Note that all the predictors are numeric, which SMOTE requires.

```{r}
#| label: show-data
#| message: false
library(recipes)
library(themis)
library(modeldata)
library(dplyr)
data("ames")

ames_imbalance <- ames |>
  filter(MS_Zoning %in% c("Residential_Low_Density", "Residential_Medium_Density")) |>
  mutate(MS_Zoning = droplevels(MS_Zoning)) |>
  select(MS_Zoning, Lot_Area, Year_Built, Gr_Liv_Area, Full_Bath)

ames_imbalance |>
  count(MS_Zoning)
```

{themis} provides `step_smote()`, which has the implementation for SMOTE.

```{r}
#| label: step_smote
recipe(MS_Zoning ~ ., data = ames_imbalance) |>
  step_smote(MS_Zoning) |>
  prep() |>
  bake(new_data = NULL) |>
  count(MS_Zoning)
```
